summary:
Artemis: Last Window is a lunar survival and resource-management game designed for children aged 7–12, playable in single-player mode or cooperatively with two players on mobile devices.

Inspired by nine real lunar regions near the Moon's south pole identified by NASA, the game challenges players to survive in a hostile environment while managing oxygen, water, food, and energy. Players must collect resources, build improvements, overcome environmental hazards, and prepare their spacecraft for the ultimate mission: returning to Earth.

Our project addresses the challenge by transforming the complexities of lunar exploration into an accessible, interactive experience. Through strategic decisions, resource management, and optional teamwork, players explore the difficulties astronauts could face when living on the Moon.

Artemis: Last Window aims to spark children's curiosity about space exploration while encouraging problem-solving, critical thinking, and collaboration, making scientific concepts more engaging through gameplay.
details:
Technical Report — ARTEMIS: Última Ventana (Lunar Blackout)

About the project

ARTEMIS: Última Ventana ("Last Window") is a 3D game in which children aged about 7 to 12 run a small base at the lunar south pole, keep the crew alive through the lunar day and night, and fly them home to Earth. It was created by team Cat-Astroficos for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026.

We answered this challenge from the Space Apps 2026 brief:

Space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies the engineering trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Few tools make those trade-offs both tangible and fun. Your challenge is to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing competing demands like life support, radiation shielding, power, and food production, so they experience firsthand the decisions that determine whether a mission fails or succeeds.

Our answer makes those trade-offs physical. Every resource is a station on the map, every trip carries one box, and a short water supply starves air, food and fuel at the same time. The balance uses NASA human-consumption rates, and the scenery uses NASA 3D models and real lunar elevation data.

The game runs on Windows PCs and Android phones, alone offline or with a partner online. It is published as a Windows build (Artemis-Ultima-Ventana.exe) and an Android test APK, release v1.0.0-android.1 (ARM64, Android 7.0 or later).

Why we built it

Children hear that humans are going back to the Moon, but few understand what it takes to stay alive there, and many of the students we want to reach only have a phone and an unreliable connection.

  • Kids don't see the trade-offs. Space content for children usually shows the Moon as an adventure with no cost, or explains life support with numbers that lose a young audience. Children rarely learn that water, air, power and food depend on each other, and that one shortage can end a mission.
  • Learning tools need good hardware. Most educational 3D games need a powerful computer or a constant internet connection. Many schools and families have only a mid-range phone, an older PC or patchy internet.
  • Our goal. Build a game that makes those trade-offs tangible and fun, accurate enough to teach real concepts, and light enough to install on a phone and play offline.

What we built

We delivered a playable lunar campaign for PC and Android, plus the art, design documents and automated tests behind it.

  1. The game. A 3D campaign with nine regions named after NASA's Artemis III candidate landing sites, solo offline play, two-player online co-op, touch controls, an Apollo-style return to Earth and an offline science archive.
  2. Builds. A Windows executable and a signed Android test APK, published as GitHub release v1.0.0-android.1.
  3. Four earlier prototypes, kept playable in the project: a 2D training academy, a turn-based outpost board, a 3D "Lunar Blackout" mission and the co-op Cresta Station. They show how the design evolved after each playtest.
  4. Art. Nine AI-assisted station models, an ice-water machine and a lunar surface; the AstroCat character built in Blender; optimized NASA models and LOLA terrain; procedural craters; and our own "paper" shader that ties it all into one style.
  5. Design documentation. A rules specification (14 November 2026), a catalogue of the nine regions, a production catalogue for modellers, a project graph linking each challenge requirement to game systems, and a parameter registry the game reads at startup.
  6. Quality tools. A one-command verification script, five regression suites and a protocol for testing the game with 12-year-old players.

What it does and how it works

The player runs a small lunar base through repeated day/night cycles and wins by launching the crew back to Earth. Every system the base needs (air, power, water, food, shielding, propellant) is a station on the map that the player must physically walk to and operate.

Core loop

  1. Gather. Mine ice and mineral at the quarry and carry them as boxes. Each box holds one item, so routes and hand-offs matter.
  2. Process. The refinery turns ice into water. Water feeds the greenhouse (food), life support (air) and the propellant plant (fuel).
  3. Power. Solar panels charge the battery during the day. At night the base runs on stored energy, and a blackout can stop production.
  4. Survive. Each astronaut has their own air and hunger meters. When a solar particle warning arrives, players must reach the shelter in time. If air hits zero, the player returns to the last dawn checkpoint without losing the profile.
  5. Return. Load three propellant batches and two rations, confirm by radio and take the seats. A 30-second countdown (cancellable) launches the ascent stage, which docks in lunar orbit before the command ship flies home.

Resource flow. The quarry produces ice and mineral, and the refinery turns ice into water. Water then feeds three stations: life support turns it into air, the greenhouse into food, and the propellant plant into fuel. The crew needs air and food to survive, while the launch pad needs three fuel loads and two rations before the trip home. Solar panels charge the battery by day, and at night every station runs on stored energy. Because almost everything starts as ice, a short water supply starves air, food and fuel at the same time.

Time and progress. A lunar day lasts 420 seconds and a night 480 seconds of play. At each dawn the game saves a checkpoint and pays coins. Coins and unlocks are shared across modes and buy access to new regions.

Modes. Solo offline: one astronaut, a pause menu and one seat needed for launch. Online co-op: two players on their own devices, connected directly over UDP (port 44260); the host's simulation is authoritative, and players pass boxes to each other.

Regions. Nine maps are named after NASA's 2024 candidate Artemis III landing regions near the lunar south pole. Mons Mouton Plateau is the starting base, and each region has its own difficulty, economy and events (for example, a radio blackout at Nobile Rim 2).

Controls. Touch-first: an on-screen joystick or tap-to-move, an Action button to operate a nearby station, and Drop / pass to hand over a box. The same controls work with a mouse on Windows.

Science archive. An in-game archive shows real mission records (for example, LRO data and historical Apollo 17 references) that work fully offline.

Benefits

The game turns abstract life-support science into decisions a young player makes with their hands, and it runs on hardware schools and families already own.

  • Learning by doing. Players see that water feeds air, food and fuel at the same time, so every trip is a trade-off. The lesson is in the mechanics, not in a text screen.
  • Grounded in real data. Consumption rates come from NASA's human metabolic references and ECLSS documentation. Region names follow NASA's Artemis III candidate list, and terrain uses LOLA elevation data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
  • Teamwork practice. Co-op mode forces two players to split roles, pass cargo and reach the shelter together, like a real crew.
  • Low barrier to entry. It installs on a mid-range Android phone (ARM64, Android 7.0+) or a Windows PC, needs no account, and the solo mode and science archive work fully offline.
  • Safe failure. Running out of air sends the player back to the last dawn instead of erasing progress, so children can experiment without frustration.
  • Bilingual-ready interface. Text is kept out of 3D models and rendered by the engine, so the game can be translated without re-modelling. The current UI is in Spanish.

Intended impact

We want children around 7 to 12 years old, especially Spanish speakers, to finish a session able to explain why a Moon base needs water, power and shelter, and to feel that Artemis-era exploration is something they could take part in.

  • Science literacy. Make the link between resources and survival intuitive: no water means no air, no food and no way home.
  • Interest in STEM careers. Put the player in the role of a crew member on a real candidate landing site, using real NASA models and data.
  • Access. Reach players who only have a phone, an older PC or no reliable internet, through a free APK, offline play and a direct-connection co-op mode.
  • Collaboration. Encourage pairs (classmates, siblings, parent and child) to plan together, communicate and share tasks.
  • Reusable foundation. Leave an open, documented project that teachers or other teams can extend with new regions, rules or languages.

A measurable goal from our test protocol: a first-time player should pass a box to a teammate within 45 seconds of play and be able to say why the crew needs to launch. This still has to be confirmed with real 12-year-old players.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

The game is written in GDScript on Godot Engine 4.7.2: about 10,400 lines across 46 scripts and one custom shader, plus Python, JavaScript and PowerShell tooling for art and testing.

Engine and languages. We built the game in Godot Engine 4.7.2, which handles the 3D scenes, physics, interface, networking and export to Windows and Android. Game logic, the simulation and the HUD are written in GDScript, and our "paper" material is written in the Godot Shading Language. On PC the game uses the Forward+ renderer (Vulkan) for soft shadows and ambient occlusion; on phones it uses the lighter GL Compatibility renderer.

Networking and movement. Online co-op uses Godot's ENet networking over UDP port 44260, with the host's game as the authority. Tap-to-move routes are calculated with Godot's AStarGrid2D pathfinding, built from the station collisions.

Tooling languages. Python 3.13 scripts generate 2D art, optimize the NASA models and build the LOLA terrain mesh. A JavaScript script on Node.js 26 rigs the cat pilots. A PowerShell script (tests/verify.ps1) runs all automated checks, and gdtoolkit 4.5.0 (gdformat and gdlint) keeps every GDScript file formatted and lint-free.

3D and art tools. Blender 5.2.2, driven by Python scripts, was used to build and animate AstroCat, reduce the NASA models and split the Apollo module into its two stages. For the station models we generated concept images with AI, turned them into textured 3D models with Tripo, and cleaned and simplified them for Godot with glTF-Transform. The 2D sprites, tiles and icons of the earlier prototypes were drawn by our own Python script using the Pillow library.

Research and reference. We used FFDec (JPEXS Flash Decompiler) to study 496 ActionScript files of an old Flash management game and understand how its build-and-expand mechanics work. NASA sources provided the Apollo Lunar Module and LRO models (NASA 3D Resources), LOLA Site06 elevation data (NASA GSFC PGDA, 5 m per pixel), the Apollo 17 photo AS17-148-22727, life-support (ECLSS) and human consumption references, and sample data from DONKI and NeoWs for the offline science archive. Third-party assets are limited to Kenney models (CC0) and the Barlow, Barlow Condensed and IBM Plex Mono fonts (OFL).

Build, version control and collaboration. The Android APK was built with the Android SDK Build-Tools, Java and Godot's export templates (ARM64, ETC2/ASTC textures, landscape). Git and GitHub hold the source history and the APK release. The team shared 3D models through a Google Drive folder and planned the base layout on a hand-drawn sketch.

AI coding assistants. OpenAI Codex and Claude Code worked as pair programmers for code, design reviews, documentation and verification runs, supported by MCP servers (filesystem, memory and sequential-thinking) and Design Game Studio skills.

Hardware. We developed on Windows laptops with AMD Radeon 760M and Intel Iris Xe graphics, ran headless tests on Linux, and target Android phones with ARM64 processors.

3D models and art: where they came from and how we made them

Most of the base was generated by the team with AI (images first, then 3D with Tripo). The space hardware and terrain come from NASA, and the characters, craters and shader were built by us.

How we produced the station models

  1. Generate a concept image of each station with an AI image generator.
  2. Convert the image into a textured 3D model with Tripo, which outputs a GLB with colour, normal and ORM (occlusion, roughness, metallic) maps.
  3. Share the model in the team's Google Drive modelos folder.
  4. Clean it for Godot with glTF-Transform: dequantize the mesh (Godot 4.7.2 cannot read KHR_mesh_quantization) and simplify very heavy meshes.
  5. Import into Godot, scale and place it on the 40 × 22 m station following the team's hand-drawn sketch, apply our paper material and add simple collision boxes.

Models made by the team with AI. The nine station models (solar panels, battery, greenhouse, rover antenna, water tank, ice deposit, ice box, pickaxe and canteen) were made from AI-generated images converted to 3D with Tripo. They are placed following the team's sketch: four solar panels and the battery to the north, a 6 m greenhouse to the west, the refinery and water tank to the south, the shelter to the east, and the ice and rover antenna to the north-east. The ice-water machine was also made with Tripo, in an empty and a full version of about 10,700 triangles each; the game shows the full one while the refinery is working. The lunar surface came from Tripo with 957,000 triangles and a 2048-pixel texture, and we simplified it to about 29,000 triangles. Our shader flattens its relief under the base and tints it lavender-grey.

Characters. AstroCat was built by the team in Blender 5.2.2 using Python scripts. We took only the cat's pose from a reference image found on Pinterest, whose original author was not recorded. The model has 9,428 triangles, 20 bones and five animations (idle, walk, run, jump and wave), and its design now drives the playable pilots. The pilot cats come from an earlier project model that we rigged with a 15-bone skeleton using our articulate_cat.mjs script, plus a shader that gives each astronaut a blue or orange suit.

NASA assets. The Apollo Lunar Module comes from NASA 3D Resources (NASA/Michael D. Carbajal). We reduced it from 97,588 to 8,472 triangles in Blender and split it into its descent and ascent stages for the return sequence. The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, also from NASA 3D Resources (NASA/Brian E. Kumanchik and Christian A. Lopez), was reduced from 8,142 to 1,701 triangles and spins in the science archive. The Nobile horizon is built from NASA GSFC PGDA LOLA Site06 elevation data at 5 m per pixel: our Python script turned a 640 × 480 pixel crop into a 1,536-triangle mesh. The Earth in the sky is a 540 × 540 copy of NASA photo AS17-148-22727, taken by Apollo 17.

Built in code and other sources. The orbital command ship for the return cinematic is a simplified Apollo command and service module made in Godot from basic shapes. The rim craters are procedural, written in GDScript, at 99 triangles each with ejecta, terraces and rocks. The radio antenna, receiver and transport ship are Kenney models (CC0 licence) from Poly Pizza, rescaled and realigned. The 2D sprites, tiles and icons of the earlier prototypes are original pixel art drawn by our Python and Pillow script (tools/draw_assets.py). The fonts are Barlow, Barlow Condensed and IBM Plex Mono under the OFL licence, which ships with the game.

NASA sources: Apollo Lunar Module, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, LOLA Site06, AS17-148-22727. Other: Kenney.

Every external file is logged in assets/props_luna/asset-register.md and assets/props_luna/nasa/procedencia.md with its author, URL and checksum. One open item: the original author of the Pinterest reference image is unknown, so we only used it as a pose reference and did not copy it.

How the project is creative

We mixed real NASA science with a toy-like, hand-crafted look and a cast of cat astronauts, so the Moon feels both authentic and inviting to children.

  • Cat astronauts. The pilots are cats in blue and orange suits. AstroCat, our guide character, was built and animated by the team in Blender from a reference pose (idle, walk, run, jump, wave), and its design now drives the playable pilots.
  • A "paper diorama" art style. We wrote our own shader (papel.gdshader) that gives every object a matte, flat-faceted, slightly grainy finish, like a cardboard model under a desk lamp. It unifies NASA models, AI-generated props and procedural craters in one style.
  • Real places as levels. Each of the nine maps is named after a real Artemis III candidate landing region. The Nobile horizon is built from actual LOLA laser-altimeter elevation data.
  • History in the finale. We split NASA's Apollo Lunar Module model into its descent and ascent stages. At launch, the descent stage stays on the Moon and the ascent stage docks in orbit, just like Apollo, while a real Apollo 17 photo of Earth glows in the sky.
  • Physical teamwork. Resources are physical boxes that hold one item each. Players carry them, drop them and pass them to each other, which turns logistics into a cooperative puzzle.
  • Procedural craters. Rim craters are generated in code with ejecta, terraces and rocks, at only 99 triangles each, so they look rich and still run on phones.
  • Learning without quizzes. There are no multiple-choice questions. The science is learned by keeping the base alive.

Factors the team considered

Every design choice was weighed against four constraints: a young audience, scientific honesty, modest hardware and responsible use of other people's work.

Age and reading level. Our players are about 7 to 12 years old, so on-screen goals are short, technical words such as "propellant" are explained the first time they appear, and warnings use text and shape, not colour alone.

Scientific accuracy versus fun. NASA consumption rates drive the balance, but capacities and timers are tuned for short sessions. Historical data and game values are stored in separate fields, and provisional numbers are flagged in the rules document.

Devices and performance. Every model has a triangle budget: the Apollo module went from 97,588 to 8,472 triangles and LRO from 8,142 to 1,701. Phones use a lighter renderer and compressed textures, with a target of 30 frames per second.

Connectivity and privacy. Solo mode needs no network. Co-op uses a direct connection with no server or account, and profiles and saves stay on the device.

Touch and accessibility. Players can use a joystick or tap to move, with two large action buttons. Failure is forgiving because the game returns to the last checkpoint, and layouts stay readable at 1152 × 648 and 1280 × 720.

Licensing and attribution. We only used CC0 models, OFL fonts and NASA media under NASA's usage guidelines. Every external file is logged with its author, URL and SHA-256 checksum.

Ethics of testing with children. Sessions are voluntary with a guardian present, notes are anonymous, and no names, photos or recordings are kept in project records.

Maintainability. Rules and parameters live in state_registry.json, so the balance can change without touching code, and assets can be regenerated from scripts.

Scope. All nine regions are specified, but they share one playable kit while each region's own terrain is produced, so the game stays shippable.

Development process and activities

We worked in short, verifiable iterations: design and record the change first, build it, run the full test suite, then log the result. The game went through 17 numbered revisions and several prototypes before reaching the current 3D campaign.

How we worked

  1. Design before code. Each iteration started by writing the plan, win/lose conditions and "adversarial" failure cases into the context_core/ knowledge base.
  2. Keep one source of truth. context_core/ holds a project graph (191 nodes and 336 edges linking challenge requirements to game systems and map zones), a parameter registry the engine reads at startup, the rules table, the architecture and an audit log.
  3. Build in small cuts. Each cut was one feature (for example, solo mode, the return cinematic or a new station layout), with AI coding assistants pairing on code and documentation under the rules in AGENTS.md.
  4. Verify every cut. tests/verify.ps1 runs formatting, linting, a clean import, a startup check and all regression suites. Visual checks were done by rendering screenshots at two resolutions.
  5. Log it. The Godot version, the checks run and their results go into changelog_audit.md, together with what is still pending.

How the prototype evolved

We started with a 2D isometric pixel-art academy (revisions 1 to 5), where players ran life support, a greenhouse and solar panels, built new modules and received visiting crews. Playtests showed the loop had too few real decisions, so revision 6 became a turn-based outpost board that balanced energy, food, air, water and radiation shielding. Its rules were clear, but it lacked action and was hard to read.

Revision 7, "Lunar Blackout", was our first 3D third-person mission: restore the power grid and rescue crop capsules. It proved that 3D movement and carrying physical cargo were fun. Revisions 8 to 13 turned it into Cresta Station, a local two-player co-op base with three selectable bases, a landing intro, NASA models and LOLA terrain. Revisions 14 to 17 built the current campaign from our 14 November rules: nine regions, online co-op, a solo offline mode, the Apollo-style return and the Android APK. The latest visual pass added the Forward+ renderer, the paper shader, crater shadows, the ice-water machine, the new 40 × 22 m station layout drawn by the team and AstroCat-style pilots.

Commit history

The work was committed to Git on 14 and 15 November 2026. On 14 November, LuisNafate published the 3D Lunar Blackout version, shipped Cresta Station with solo and local co-op, added the lunar base campaign and its animated intro, integrated the optimized NASA models and LOLA relief, recorded clean import and runtime checks, implemented the campaign rules and crater scenery, added the offline single-player mode, aligned the terrain with an Apollo-style return, and documented the Android APK delivery. On 15 November, Luvia Magali Hidalgo Garcia switched the PC version to Forward+ with the paper shader, shaded craters and the ice-water machine, and then delivered the new station layout with the team's own assets, the 40 × 22 m map and the AstroCat pilot.

Testing and verification

The last full Windows run (revision 16) passed formatting and linting of 45 scripts, a clean import, a startup check and five regression suites with zero failures.

The lunar campaign suite ran 8 cases and 419 assertions, covering solo and two-player online sessions, saves, radio, launch and return, and it also passed when rendered at 1152 × 648 and 1280 × 720. The academy suite ran 16 cases and 3,884 assertions on the 2D training mission, building, crews, failures and restart. The Cresta Station suite ran 10 cases and 285 assertions on local co-op with simulated keyboard input, both win routes and launch. The outpost board suite ran 7 cases and 75 assertions on turn forecasts, repairs, defeat and victory. The Lunar Blackout suite ran 3 cases and 35 assertions on restoring the grid, jumps, routes and time-out losses.

Other checks

  • Terrain audit. All 14 operation points and both spawn points were checked. The 54 crater footprints across the nine bases stay outside walkable areas, and the longest route to the shelter is 14.95 m.
  • Independent model. A separate Python model reproduced the outpost board's winning routes to confirm the simulation math.
  • Builds. The Windows x64 export launched and exited with code 0. The APK's signature and manifest were verified with Android SDK Build-Tools.
  • Expert usability review. We applied our own child-testing protocol (tools/skills/probar-juego-con-ninos), which led us to explain "propellant" and to separate "no signal" from "no light" in the UI.

Known gaps. The two most recent visual cuts were checked by eye on Windows and in headless runs on Linux, where the campaign suite reports 17 solo-mode failures (the same before and after those changes). The campaign and Cresta suites still need updating for the new pilot model and station layout.

Current status and next steps

The game is playable end to end on Windows, and an Android test APK is published. The main open items are a real-phone test and the first sessions with young players.

  • Install and play the APK on a physical Android phone and confirm the 30 fps target
  • Update the campaign and Cresta test suites for the new pilots and the 40 × 22 m layout, then rerun tests/verify.ps1 on Windows
  • Run observed first sessions with 12-year-old players and measure the 45-second hand-off goal
  • Build each region's own terrain (the nine regions currently share one playable kit)
  • Decide the pending balance values: solar booster effect, night battery cost (rule REC-E7), exposure effects and pause behaviour in online play
  • Translate the interface into English
